```text
/* the <aria-menu> web component, styled to match ".ui.dropdown .menu" so migrated menus look the same */
aria-menu {
  display: inline-flex;
  align-items: center;
  vertical-align: middle;
  position: relative;
  font-size: 1rem;
  line-height: var(--line-height-default);
  text-align: left;
}

aria-menu > :not(.menu) {
  cursor: pointer;
  user-select: none;
}

/* normalize.css gives buttons line-height 1.15, and browsers reset their font weight */
aria-menu > .btn {
  line-height: inherit;
  font-weight: inherit;
}

/* like ".ui.dropdown > .text > img", an image before the trigger text keeps its gap */
aria-menu > .btn > img,
aria-menu > .btn > .img {
  margin-right: 0.78571429rem;
}

/* a ".ui.button" trigger keeps the caret where ".ui.dropdown.button" put it, in the right padding */
aria-menu > .ui.button:has(> .dropdown.icon) {
  position: relative;
  padding-right: 22px;
}

aria-menu > .ui.tiny.button:has(> .dropdown.icon) {
  padding-right: 20px;
}

aria-menu > .ui.button > .dropdown.icon {
  position: absolute;
  top: 50%;
  right: 0.5em;
  transform: translateY(-50%);
}

/* like ".ui.active.dropdown.button", a neutral button trigger looks pressed while its menu is open */
aria-menu > .ui.button:not(.primary, .red, .green)[aria-expanded="true"] {
  background: var(--color-active);
}

aria-menu > .menu {
  position: absolute;
  top: 100%;
  left: 0;
  z-index: 11;
  min-width: max-content;
  margin: 0;
  padding: 0;
  background: var(--color-menu);
  color: var(--color-text);
  border: 1px solid var(--color-secondary);
  border-radius: var(--border-radius);
  box-shadow: 0 6px 18px var(--color-shadow);
  text-align: left;
  cursor: auto;
}

aria-menu[placement$="-end"] > .menu {
  left: auto;
  right: 0;
}

aria-menu[placement^="top-"] > .menu {
  top: auto;
  bottom: 100%;
  border-radius: var(--border-radius) var(--border-radius) 0 0;
}

/* "floating" matches ".ui.floating.dropdown": a gap from the trigger and all corners rounded */
aria-menu[floating] > .menu {
  border-radius: var(--border-radius);
}

aria-menu[floating]:not([placement^="top-"]) > .menu {
  margin-top: 0.5em;
}

aria-menu[floating][placement^="top-"] > .menu {
  margin-bottom: 0.5em;
}

aria-menu[pointing]:not([placement^="top-"]) > .menu {
  margin-top: 1em;
}

aria-menu[pointing]:not([placement^="top-"]) > .menu::after {
  content: "";
  position: absolute;
  top: -0.25em;
  left: 1em;
  width: 0.5em;
  height: 0.5em;
  transform: rotate(45deg);
  background: var(--color-menu);
  box-shadow: -1px -1px 0 0 var(--color-secondary);
  z-index: 2;
  pointer-events: none;
}

aria-menu[pointing][placement$="-end"] > .menu::after {
  left: auto;
  right: 1em;
}

/* the element upgrades in <head> but only sets up its children at DOMContentLoaded, keep the popup hidden until then */
aria-menu > .menu:not([role="menu"]) {
  display: none;
}

aria-menu > .menu > .item {
  display: block;
  min-height: 2.57142857rem;
  padding: 0.78571429rem 1.14285714rem;
  font-size: 1rem;
  color: var(--color-text);
  font-weight: var(--font-weight-normal); /* not a surrounding header's weight */
  line-height: var(--line-height-default);
  white-space: nowrap;
  cursor: pointer;
  text-decoration: none;
}

aria-menu > .menu > .item > svg {
  margin-right: 0.78rem;
}

aria-menu > .menu > .item > img {
  display: inline-block;
  vertical-align: top;
  width: auto;
  max-height: 2em;
  margin: -0.25rem 0.78571429rem -0.25rem 0;
}

aria-menu > .menu > .item:first-child {
  border-radius: var(--border-radius) var(--border-radius) 0 0;
}

aria-menu > .menu > .item:last-child {
  border-radius: 0 0 var(--border-radius) var(--border-radius);
}

aria-menu > .menu > .item:hover:not(.active, :active),
aria-menu > .menu > .item:focus-visible,
aria-menu > .menu > .item.selected {
  background: var(--color-hover);
}

aria-menu > .menu > .item:focus {
  outline: none;
}

aria-menu > .menu > .item.active,
aria-menu > .menu > .item:active {
  background: var(--color-active);
}

aria-menu > .menu > .item:focus-visible {
  outline: 2px solid var(--color-primary);
  outline-offset: -2px;
}

aria-menu > .menu > .divider {
  border-top: 1px solid var(--color-secondary);
  height: 0;
  margin: 4px 0;
}

aria-menu > .menu > .header {
  margin: 1rem 0 0.75rem;
  padding: 0 1.14285714rem;
  font-size: 0.95em;
  font-weight: var(--font-weight-medium);
}

  });

  test('removing an open menu resets its state', () => {
    const {root, menu, trigger, popup, cleanup} = renderMenu();
    press(trigger, 'Enter');
    menu.remove();
    expect(isOpen(trigger, popup)).toBe(false);

    expect(document.activeElement).toBe(after);
    cleanup();

});

describe('AC6 activation', () => {
  for (const [name, activate] of [
    ['Enter', (item: HTMLElement) => press(item, 'Enter')],
    ['Space', (item: HTMLElement) => press(item, ' ')],

  ] as const) {
    test(`${name} runs the item's click handler and closes`, () => {
      const {trigger, popup, items, cleanup} = renderMenu();
      const handler = vi.fn();

      expect(document.activeElement).toBe(trigger);
      cleanup();
    });
  }

  test('focus moved by the handler is kept', () => {
    const {root, trigger, items, cleanup} = renderMenu();
    const after = root.querySelector<HTMLElement>('.after')!;
    items[0].addEventListener('click', () => after.focus());
    press(trigger, 'Enter');
    press(items[0], 'Enter');
    expect(document.activeElement).toBe(after);
    cleanup();
  });
});

    test(`${name} on a disabled item does nothing and leaves the menu open`, () => {
      const {root, trigger, popup, items, cleanup} = renderWithDisabled();
      const handler = vi.fn();
      const delegated = vi.fn();
      items[1].addEventListener('click', handler);
      root.addEventListener('click', delegated); // like the document-level "link-action" handler
      press(trigger, 'Enter');
      items[1].focus();
      activate(items[1]);
      expect(handler).not.toHaveBeenCalled();
      expect(delegated).not.toHaveBeenCalled();
      expect(isOpen(trigger, popup)).toBe(true);
      expect(document.activeElement).toBe(items[1]);
      cleanup();
    });
  }
});

  const trigger = page.getByRole('button', {name: 'Add Webhook'});
  const menu = page.getByRole('menu', {name: 'Add Webhook'});

  await trigger.focus();
  await page.keyboard.press('Enter');
  await expect(trigger).toHaveAttribute('aria-expanded', 'true');
  await expect(page.getByRole('menuitem', {name: 'Gitea'})).toBeFocused();
  await page.keyboard.press('End');
  await expect(page.getByRole('menuitem', {name: 'Packagist'})).toBeFocused();
  await page.keyboard.press('Escape');

  await expect(page.getByRole('menuitem', {name: 'DingTalk'})).toBeFocused();
  // the button sits at the header's right edge, so the menu must open leftwards from it
  const triggerBox = (await trigger.boundingBox())!;
  const menuBox = (await menu.boundingBox())!;
  expect(menuBox.x + menuBox.width).toBeCloseTo(triggerBox.x + triggerBox.width, 0);

export async function createProjectColumn(requestContext: APIRequestContext, owner: string, repo: string, projectID: string, title: string) {
  await apiRetry(() => requestContext.post(`${baseUrl()}/${owner}/${repo}/projects/${projectID}/columns/new`, {
    headers: apiHeaders(),
    form: {title},
  }), 'createProjectColumn');
}

export async function apiDeleteRepo(requestContext: APIRequestContext, owner: string, name: string) {
  await apiRetry(() => requestContext.delete(`${baseUrl()}/api/v1/repos/${owner}/${name}`, {
    headers: apiHeaders(),
  }), 'apiDeleteRepo');
}

export async function createProject(
  page: Page,
  {owner, repo, title}: {owner: string; repo: string; title: string},
): Promise<{id: number}> {
  // Navigate to new project page
  await page.goto(`/${owner}/${repo}/projects/new`);

  // Fill in project details
  await page.getByLabel('Title').fill(title);

  // Submit the form
  await page.getByRole('button', {name: 'Create Project'}).click();

  // Wait for redirect to projects list
  await page.waitForURL(new RegExp(`/${owner}/${repo}/projects$`));

  // Extract the project ID from the project link in the list
  const projectLink = page.locator('.milestone-list > .item').filter({hasText: title}).locator('a').first();
  const href = await projectLink.getAttribute('href');
  const match = /\/projects\/(\d+)/.exec(href || '');
  const id = match ? parseInt(match[1]) : 0;

  return {id};
}

export async function apiCreateFile(requestContext: APIRequestContext, owner: string, repo: string, filepath: string, content: string, {branch, newBranch, message}: {branch?: string; newBranch?: string; message?: string} = {}) {
  await apiRetry(() => requestContext.post(`${baseUrl()}/api/v1/repos/${owner}/${repo}/contents/${filepath}`, {
    headers: apiHeaders(),
    data: {content: Buffer.from(content, 'utf8').toString('base64'), branch, new_branch: newBranch, message},
  }), 'apiCreateFile');
}

test('project column menu opens the edit dialog by keyboard without moving the column', async ({page, request}) => {
  const repoName = `e2e-column-menu-${randomString(8)}`;
  await Promise.all([apiCreateRepo(request, {name: repoName}), login(page)]);
  const {id} = await createProject(page, {owner, repo: repoName, title: 'Board'});
  for (const title of ['First', 'Second']) {
    await createProjectColumn(request, owner, repoName, String(id), title);
  }
  await page.goto(`/${owner}/${repoName}/projects/${id}`);
  const columnIds = () => page.locator('#project-board > .project-column').evaluateAll((els) => els.map((el) => el.getAttribute('data-id')));
  const before = await columnIds();
  const column = page.locator('.project-column').filter({hasText: 'Second'});
  const trigger = column.getByRole('button', {name: 'More Operations'});

  // a mouse press on the menu sits inside the column's drag handle, and must open the menu instead
  await trigger.click();
  await expect(trigger).toHaveAttribute('aria-expanded', 'true');
  await page.keyboard.press('Escape');
  await expect(trigger).toBeFocused();

  await page.keyboard.press('Enter');
  await expect(column.getByRole('menuitem', {name: 'Edit Column'})).toBeFocused();
  await page.keyboard.press('Enter');
  await expect(page.locator('#project-column-modal-edit')).toBeVisible();
  await expect(page.locator('#project-column-modal-edit input[name="title"]')).toHaveValue('Second');
  expect(await columnIds()).toEqual(before);
  await assertNoJsError(page);
});

test('run row menu cancels a run by keyboard', async ({page, request}) => {
  const repoName = `e2e-run-menu-${randomString(8)}`;

  // with no runner the run stays waiting, so it can be cancelled

  const run = page.locator('.run-list > .item').first();

});

```markdown
Closes #109

## What changed

The four remaining "…" row menus outside the issue sidebar move from Fomantic dropdowns to `<aria-menu>`: the workflow menu and each run row on the Actions tab, each project column, and each package cleanup rule. `<aria-menu>` also learns disabled items.

- `web_src/js/webcomponents/aria-menu.ts`: an `.item.disabled` child gets `aria-disabled="true"`, refreshed on every open. The arrow keys still reach it. Enter, Space and click on it do nothing and leave the menu open: a capture-phase click guard stops the item's own handlers and delegated ones such as `link-action`.
- `web_src/css/modules/aria-menu.css`: disabled items are dimmed like `.ui.menu .item.disabled`, with no hover background, but stay focusable.
- `templates/repo/actions/list.tmpl`, `runs_list.tmpl`, `templates/projects/view.tmpl`, `templates/package/shared/cleanup_rules/list.tmpl`: each menu is now `<aria-menu placement="bottom-end">` with a `<button type="button" aria-label="More Operations">` trigger. Every `link-action`, `show-modal`, `data-modal-*` and `data-modal-confirm` attribute is kept. The project column items drop their Fomantic `button` class, and the run menu drops `flex-items-menu`, which only applied inside `.ui.dropdown`.
- `web_src/js/features/repo-projects.ts`: the column Sortable gets `filter: 'aria-menu'` and `preventOnFilter: false`. A press on the menu, which sits inside the `.project-column-header` drag handle, never starts a drag and still focuses and clicks the button.

## Why

Keyboard and screen reader users couldn't reliably operate these menus (#109). This covers the acceptance criteria:

- **AC1:** the workflow and run row menus are `<aria-menu>` with no Fomantic `dropdown` class, and each trigger is named "More Operations".
- **AC2:** project column Edit opens the column modal, and "Set as default" and "Delete" keep their `data-modal-confirm-*` dialogs.
- **AC3:** cleanup rule Edit and Preview remain plain links.
- **AC4:** disabled items as above.
- **AC5:** "Disable workflow" for a required workflow already rendered as `.item.disabled` with no `data-url`. It is now announced as dimmed and inert. For a workflow that isn't required, the item is unchanged.
- **AC6:** the keyboard behaviour comes from the shared component.
- **AC7:** the Sortable filter.
- **AC8:** see below.

## How it was tested

- **Vitest** (`web_src/js/webcomponents/aria-menu.test.ts`, new `disabled items` block, AC4):
  - a disabled item gets `aria-disabled="true"` and ArrowDown reaches it
  - an item enabled after init loses the mark on the next open
  - for each of Enter, Space and click: neither the item's own handler nor a delegated ancestor handler runs, the menu stays open, and focus stays on the item

  I confirmed the four behaviour tests fail with the component change reverted.
- **Playwright** (`tests/e2e/row-menus.test.ts`):
  - *Project column (AC2, AC6, AC7):* a mouse click on a column's "More Operations" opens the menu instead of starting a drag. Escape returns focus. Enter puts focus on "Edit Column", Enter opens the edit dialog with the column's title, and the column order is unchanged.
  - *Run row (AC1, AC6):* pushing a workflow with no runner leaves a waiting run. Its "More Operations" opens by keyboard on "View workflow file", ArrowDown reaches "Cancel workflow run", and Enter cancels it (`data-status="cancelled"`).
- **Existing suites:** `menus.test.ts`, `webhook-menus.test.ts` and `repo-menus.test.ts` re-run, since Decision 2 changes the shared component that the navbar, comment, webhook and repo menus use.
- **Not automated:**
  - The required-workflow "Disable workflow" case (AC5) needs an organisation-level required workflow. The disabled behaviour itself is covered by the Vitest tests.
  - The cleanup rule menu (AC3) is two plain links.

## CI / manual verification

Run locally on this branch:

- `pnpm exec vitest run web_src/js/webcomponents/aria-menu`: 28 passed
- `GITEA_TEST_E2E_FLAGS='tests/e2e/row-menus.test.ts tests/e2e/menus.test.ts tests/e2e/webhook-menus.test.ts tests/e2e/repo-menus.test.ts' make test-e2e`: E2E_RESULT
- ESLint on the changed TS files, stylelint on `aria-menu.css`, `vue-tsc --noEmit`, `make lint-templates`: clean

## Design

As in the issue's Design Decisions. Decision 1: rebuild all four menus as `<aria-menu>`. Decision 2: disabled items stay focusable but inert. Decision 3: Sortable's `filter` keeps the column menu out of drag-and-drop.

## Tech Debt

**Introduced:**
- A run list renders one `<aria-menu>`, each with its own listeners, per row. That is fine at the page size, as the issue's Decision 1 notes. An unpaginated list would want one delegated menu.
- Any later interactive control placed in a project column header has to be added to the Sortable `filter` too.

**Encountered:**
- `flex-items-menu` and the items' `button` class only styled Fomantic dropdowns, so they silently stopped applying once the menus moved. I removed them rather than leave dead classes behind.
- ESLint's `unicorn/prefer-toggle-attribute` suggests `toggleAttribute`, which writes `aria-disabled=""`. ARIA treats that as not disabled, so the code removes the attribute and sets it explicitly, with a comment saying why.

I reviewed every line, operated the menus by hand, and can explain each change. AI log: see the AI Assistance comment on #109.

**Decision:** Add `filter: 'aria-menu'` and `preventOnFilter: false` to the column Sortable in `web_src/js/features/repo-projects.ts`, so a press that starts on the menu never begins a drag but still focuses and clicks the menu's button.

**Alternatives Considered:**
- (a) Stop the menu's pointer events from propagating, inside `<aria-menu>`.
- (b) Move the menu out of `.project-column-header`.

**Rationale:** (a) puts board-specific code in the shared component, and it would also block the delegated `link-action`/`show-modal` handlers that rely on events bubbling up to `document`. (b) changes the column header's layout and moves the menu away from where users expect it. Sortable's `filter` option is designed for controls inside a drag handle: SortableJS 1.15.7 matches the press target's closest `aria-menu` and cancels the drag. It is a two-line change in the one file that owns the board. `preventOnFilter` defaults to `true`, which would call `preventDefault()` on the press and stop the button from taking focus, so it is turned off.

**Consequences:** Easier: `<aria-menu>` stays generic, and the column header keeps its layout. Harder: any later interactive control added to the column header must also be added to the filter, or pressing it will start a drag.

'''

## UML diagrams (D6)

The person who resolved a medium issue draws a class diagram and a sequence diagram for it. Several

**Class diagram:**

1. Among all the classes shown in the diagram, which 1--2 are most central to understanding the codebase and solving the issue? Explain what role each one plays.

3. Looking back at your implementation, is there anything in this design you would change, and why?

**Sequence diagram:**

1. What user action or system event starts the sequence, and what is the expected outcome when it completes successfully?
2. Identify the 2--3 most important steps in the sequence. For each one, describe what is happening and note whether it involves existing code or new/modified code from your solution.
3. What error cases or alternative paths are not shown in the diagram, and why did you leave them out?

# Report: Sprint 2

**Team Name:** GiCoffee

**Team member names:** Vishav Chopra (vvchopra), Carson Rackley (CarsonRackley), Arjun Bhat (arjunsb26), Aman Bhoot (ab-wm), Jack Donohue (Jack-Donohue), Ethan Turner (controlled-opposition)

**Project Name:** Gitea

**Project Link:** [https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/gitea](https://github.com/CSCI-435-SE/gitea)

## Sprint Overview

### What we planned to do

Sprint 2 started from the Sprint 1 carryovers. The keyboard-shortcut sub-issues of #23 (#56–#60, plus #95), the dropdown regression suite from #25 (#65), notification sorting from #7 (#52), and the PostgreSQL failure in #77's burndown test all went into the backlog first, as the Sprint 1 plan said they would.

The shortcut work was planned in dependency order. #56 replaces Gitea's single page-wide key handler with a central shortcut registry, and #57, #58, #59, #60 and #95 all build on it, so #56 had to merge first. The rest of the team took new medium issues so that every CSCI 435 member owned at least two:

- Calendar deadlines (#36), split into #98 and #100
- More `<aria-menu>` migrations and an ARIA bug under #25 (#104, #108, #109, #110)
- A second notifications feature under #7 (#117)
- A milestone follow-up to Sprint 1's burndown chart (#131)

### Scope changes

- **#52 depended on #117.** #52's sort had to work inside #117's repository groups, so #117 was written and merged first (PR #120), and #52 followed in PR #122.
- **#118 was deferred to Sprint 3.** The tab badge and desktop notifications issue under #7 was taken off the milestone. Its owner explained on the issue that #52's migration and notifier changes left no time to finish it this sprint.
- **#101 and #102 were left off the milestone.** #36 was split into four issues: the calendar view (#98) and the public iCalendar feed (#100) were kept for this sprint, and the private-repository feed with revocable tokens (#101) and the personal cross-repository feed (#102) were left for later.

In total, 14 of the 16 issues on the Sprint 2 milestone are closed, each by a merged PR. The PostgreSQL burndown fix was merged as PR #125.

| #56–#60 keyboard shortcuts (deferred from Sprint 1) | Taken. All five merged: #96, #115, #97, #114 and #121. |
| #65 Playwright keyboard regression suite for dropdowns | Taken. Merged in PR #105. |
| #77's burndown test failing on PostgreSQL | Taken. Fixed in PR #125: changes made within the same second are now ordered by issue, oldest first, so the result no longer depends on the database's row order. |

## Requirements & Design

### Were specs complete before coding started?

Yes. Every issue was written in the course format: User Story, User Scenario, numbered Acceptance Criteria, Out of Scope, Open Questions and Design Decisions. Every issue also got a "Spec reviewed" comment from a teammate before its PR was opened:

- The shortcut and test issues (#56–#60, #65, #95) were reviewed on Oct 18, the day #56's PR was opened.
- The later issues (#52, #98, #100, #104, #108, #110, #117) were reviewed between Oct 26 and Oct 27, before or on the day their PRs were opened.

This sprint, reviewers checked each spec against the code, not just its wording. That caught real problems before implementation:

- **#104:** the review found that the planned fix, wrapping the dropdown's `onHide`, would never run for the label picker, because the picker later replaces `onHide` with its own setting. Decision 1 was changed before any code was written.
- **#108:** the commit page's cherry-pick, branch and tag dialogs sit inside the menu being migrated. `<aria-menu>` treats typed keys as type-ahead, so moving them as-is would have broken typing a branch or tag name. The modals were moved out of the menu, and an acceptance criterion was added for it.
- **#52:** the review found that repository transfer notifications never pass through the code that sets a reason. It also suggested storing the reason as a number that matches its rank, so "Sort: Reason" is a plain `ORDER BY` that keeps paging and #117's grouping working. Both points became design decisions.
- **#58 and #59** were approved with empty Design Decision sections. Their decisions were recorded in comments on the issues during implementation instead of in the issue bodies.

**Surprises:**

- **The cost of #52's migration.** Storing a reason on every notification needed a migration plus changes to how the notifier queues each kind of notification. That was a large part of why #118 was deferred.
- **#117 and #52 overlapped.** #52's sort had to work inside #117's groups, so #52 was redesigned (its Decision 5) after #117 merged.
- **#100 added a dependency.** It brought in the first new Go library of the sprint, `golang-ical`. Its spec recorded the alternatives (a hand-written serializer and `emersion/go-ical`) and the fallback if the dependency was rejected.

### Key design decisions

Every implemented issue records at least one decision with two or more alternatives, as D3 requires.

- **#56:** All shortcuts are kept in one registry in the page code, and a shortcut can be scoped to part of the page, instead of being found through `<kbd>` hints in the HTML. This is what made two-key sequences such as `g i` possible.
- **#57:** The help dialog uses the native `<dialog>` element, and its markup and text are rendered on the server so they can be translated.
- **#60:** The on/off setting is stored in the browser, and `?` keeps working when shortcuts are off, so the user can always turn them back on.
- **#65:** ARIA state is asserted in Playwright, by extending the existing label picker and navbar tests rather than adding a new suite.
- **#95:** `r` shares one quoting helper with the existing "Quote reply" menu item, and it is only registered on pages that have a reply box.
- **#98:** The month grid is rendered on the server with a Go template, reusing the deadline bounds from Sprint 1's #34. Month navigation and filters are plain links.
- **#100:** The iCalendar feeds are generated with `golang-ical` and served from new handlers in `routers/web/feed/`, behind the same `feedEnabled` guard and permission check as the RSS and Atom feeds. Private repositories return 404 until #101 adds tokens.
- **#104:** The ARIA state is refreshed when the dropdown module's own `hide` runs, rather than through `onHide`, which the label picker overrides.
- **#108 and #110:** Only action menus move to `<aria-menu>`. Menus that show a current selection, like Sort and Filter, stay on Fomantic. #110 records why the webhook type switcher still counts as an action menu.
- **#117:** Grouping is done in the SQL query, not on the page, so each repository's rows stay together across pages. Sections are ordered A–Z, the choice lives in the URL like Sprint 1's #50 filters, and collapsed sections are kept in page memory so a live refresh doesn't reopen them.
- **#52:** The reason is stored in a new column as a number that matches its priority, and the highest-priority reason wins. Existing notifications get "Other" and sort last, and the sort works inside #117's groups.

## Test Strategy

As in Sprint 1, tests were written against each acceptance criterion:

- **Go unit tests** for models, services and handlers: #120, #122, #123, #125, #129
- **Integration tests** through the full HTTP request path: #120, #122, #123, #128, #129
- **Vitest** frontend unit tests: #96, #97, #114, #115, #116, #120, #121, #124
- **Playwright end-to-end tests**: #96, #97, #105, #114, #115, #116, #120, #121, #124, #127, #128

The shortcut PRs are mostly frontend, so they lean on Vitest for the registry logic and on Playwright for real key presses on real pages. #52's migration has its own migration test with fixtures (`v345_test.go`). #125 fixed a test that failed only on PostgreSQL by making the code's ordering deterministic, rather than loosening the test.

Changes we couldn't test automatically:

- **Screen reader output** can't be driven in CI. The `<aria-menu>` and ARIA work (#104, #108, #110, #65) asserts ARIA attributes and roles instead.
- **Real calendar apps** can't subscribe to a CI server. #129 tests the feed builder (`services/feed/ical_test.go`) and the endpoints (`tests/integration/repo_ical_test.go`), but not how a calendar app displays the feed.
- **Visual layout** of new UI was checked by hand and with light and dark screenshots in `docs/sprint2/screenshots/` (#52, #57, #60, #95).
- **Firefox and WebKit** end-to-end runs happen only in CI.

## Risks and Retrospective

### What worked

- **Building the registry first.** Merging #56 first turned five more shortcut features (#57–#60, #95) into small PRs that each added a few registry entries and could be reviewed on their own.
- **Spec reviews that read the code.** These caught design problems in #104, #108 and #52 before any code was written, which is cheaper than finding them in PR review.
- **Sprint 1 changes that stuck.** AI logs went in separate PRs, specs were approved before branches were started, and the PostgreSQL test failure carried over from Sprint 1 was fixed (#125).
- **Screenshots for UI changes.** These were committed in light and dark mode under `docs/sprint2/screenshots/`, which made UI PRs quicker to review.

### What slowed the team down

- **PRs still bunched up at the end.** 12 of the 15 code PRs were opened on or after Oct 24, and six of them (#122, #123, #124, #127, #128, #129) merged in the last two days. Our Sprint 1 goal of opening PRs by mid-sprint was met only by the first shortcut PRs (#96 and #97).
- **Specs were written late.** Most of the new issues (#98, #100, #104, #108, #109, #110) were written on Oct 22, and #117 on Oct 26, so the write, review and implement cycle for them fit into the last week.
- **Review load fell on one person.** ab-wm reviewed 9 of the 15 code PRs. Spreading reviews more evenly would have shortened the wait at the end.
- **CI trouble around #114.** After #114 merged, a revert (#119) was opened to get CI passing and then closed without merging.
- **#52's migration.** Adding a column to every notification row and changing the notifier queue was more work than its medium estimate suggested, which pushed #118 into Sprint 3.

### Changes for Sprint 3

- Write and review every Sprint 3 spec in the first three days of the sprint.
- Open each member's first PR by the middle of the sprint.
- Spread reviews so that each member reviews at least two PRs, and name the reviewer when the PR is opened.
- Size issues that need a migration or a queue change as large, or split them.

## Sprint 3 Plan

Carryover and follow-up issues:

- **#118** (CarsonRackley): tab icon badge and opt-in desktop notifications, deferred from Sprint 2, which finishes #7.
- **#101 and #102** (#36): private repository feeds with a revocable calendar token, and one personal deadline feed across all of a user's repositories, building on #100.

# Issue #117 -- Group notifications by repository

## Class Diagram

![Class diagram](117-CarsonRackley-class.png)

Grey boxes are existing code I found during concept location and impact analysis. Blue boxes marked ✎ were modified by PR #120, and green boxes marked ★ are new. Inside a box, ★ and ✎ after a member mark the members that were added or changed. The amber notes explain the design decisions from #117.

Only the classes and members that matter for the feature are shown; unrelated fields and methods are left out.

**Go to UML:** Go has no classes, so each struct is drawn as a class with its fields and methods. Go interfaces are satisfied implicitly, without an `implements` keyword, so `FindNotificationOptions` satisfying `db.FindOptions` is drawn as a dashed realization arrow. `FindNotificationOptions` embeds `db.ListOptions`, shown as an «embedded» member; it supplies the paging methods that, together with `ToConds()`, satisfy `db.FindOptions`. `db.Find` also calls `ToJoins()` and `ToOrders()` when the options type defines them. Package-level functions, such as the route handlers and `CountNotificationsByRepo`, are grouped in «functions» boxes, and the TypeScript file is a «module» box.

The Mermaid sources are `117-CarsonRackley-class.mmd` and `117-CarsonRackley-sequence.mmd`.

## Sequence Diagram

![Sequence diagram](117-CarsonRackley-sequence.png)

Steps in green boxes are new code from PR #120, and steps in the blue box use modified code. Everything else is existing code. ★ and ✎ in a message mark a new or changed call. The diagram shows the main success path for one page of grouped notifications.

## Q&A

**Class diagram:**

1. Among all the classes shown in the diagram, which 1--2 are most central to understanding the codebase and solving the issue? Explain what role each one plays.

   `FindNotificationOptions` and `notificationGroup`. `FindNotificationOptions` controls the database query: with `GroupByRepo` on, it joins the repository table and sorts by repository, so each repo's notifications come back together. `notificationGroup` is the new struct that holds one repository's section on the page: the repo, its unread count, and its notifications.

2. What is the most significant relationship shown in the diagram? Explain what it represents in the system and why it matters for understanding the solution.

```mjs
// usage: node render-mmd.mjs <repo-root> <in.mmd> <out.png>
import {readFileSync} from 'node:fs';
import {createRequire} from 'node:module';
import {resolve} from 'node:path';

const [root, input, output] = process.argv.slice(2);
const require = createRequire(resolve(root, 'package.json'));
const {chromium} = require('@playwright/test');
const mermaidJs = readFileSync(resolve(root, 'node_modules/mermaid/dist/mermaid.min.js'), 'utf8');
const code = readFileSync(input, 'utf8');

const browser = await chromium.launch();
const page = await browser.newPage({deviceScaleFactor: 2, viewport: {width: 1600, height: 1200}});
await page.setContent('<!doctype html><html><body style="margin:0;background:#fff"><div id="out" style="display:inline-block;padding:24px;background:#fff"></div></body></html>');
await page.addScriptTag({content: mermaidJs});
const error = await page.evaluate(async (src) => {
  try {
    window.mermaid.initialize({startOnLoad: false, theme: 'default', securityLevel: 'strict'});
    const {svg} = await window.mermaid.render('diagram', src);
    document.querySelector('#out').innerHTML = svg;
    return null;
  } catch (e) {
    return String(e?.message ?? e);
  }
}, code);
if (error) {
  console.error(`render failed: ${error}`);
  await browser.close();
  process.exit(1);
}
await page.locator('#out').screenshot({path: output});
await browser.close();
console.log(`wrote ${output}`);

```

```markdown
# Issue #131 -- Show each open milestone's projected finish on the milestones list

## Class Diagram

![Class diagram](131-arjunsb26-class.png)

Grey boxes are existing code I found during concept location and impact analysis, mostly the burndown service from #14. Blue boxes marked ✎ were modified by PR #134, and green boxes marked ★ are new. Inside a box, ★ and ✎ before a member mark the members that were added or changed. The amber notes explain the two design decisions from #131 and the scope limit raised in the spec review.

Only the classes and members that matter for the feature are shown. `MilestoneBurndown`'s ideal line and change lists, for example, are left out.

**Go to UML:** Go has no classes, so each struct is drawn as a class with its fields. Package-level functions, such as the route handlers, the burndown service and `NewMilestoneProjection`, are grouped in «functions» boxes named after their package. `BurndownStatus` is a named `string` type with a set of constants, so it is drawn as an «enumeration». A Go pointer field or return value (`*int`, `*MilestoneProjection`) can be nil, so it is drawn with multiplicity 0..1. `translation.Locale` is a Go interface, which the template reaches through `ctx.Locale`. No type in this diagram embeds another struct; an embedded field would be drawn as an «embedded» member. The template and the TypeScript file aren't Go types, so they are drawn as «template» and «module» boxes.

The Mermaid sources are `131-arjunsb26-class.mmd` and `131-arjunsb26-sequence.mmd`.

## Sequence Diagram

![Sequence diagram](131-arjunsb26-sequence.png)

Steps in green boxes are new code from PR #134, and steps in blue boxes use modified code. Everything else is existing code. ★ and ✎ in a message mark a new or changed call. Step 9 is a new call site for an existing service. The diagram shows the main success path for one page of open milestones.

## Q&A

**Class diagram:**

1. Among all the classes shown in the diagram, which 1--2 are most central to understanding the codebase and solving the issue? Explain what role each one plays.

   `MilestoneBurndown` and `MilestoneProjection`.
   - `MilestoneBurndown` already existed from #14. It is the result of replaying a milestone's history, and its `Status`, `Projected` and `DaysLate` fields already hold the answer the list needs, so the feature never recomputes a projection.
   - `MilestoneProjection` is the new struct between that result and the page. It holds locale keys and numbers, not finished text, so the template can render the chart's own sentence in the viewer's language. That's how the list and the chart say the same thing (AC5) without adding any new strings.

2. What is the most significant relationship shown in the diagram? Explain what it represents in the system and why it matters for understanding the solution.

   Both handlers depend on the new `burndownOptions` helper. That dependency holds the permission rule: count issues if the viewer can read them, and count pull requests only if the viewer can read them (and only by default for someone who can read nothing else). The route lets in a reader of either kind, so a check on the route alone isn't enough. In #14 I learned that a reader of issues only could otherwise see pull request titles in the chart. Before this PR, the rule lived inline in `MilestoneBurndownData`. Copying it into `Milestones` would have let the two drift apart, so both now call the one helper, and AC6's integration tests turn each unit off to check that nothing leaks.

3. Looking back at your implementation, is there anything in this design you would change, and why?

   The rule that picks a sentence from the status now exists twice: in Go (`NewMilestoneProjection`) and in TypeScript (`burndownSummary`), shown by the "mirrors" arrow. A new status or a change in wording has to touch both. With more time, I would have the server send the chart its summary key too, so there is only one copy. That changes #14's chart, which is why it was out of scope here. I'd also look at the per-milestone cost: each open milestone on the page runs three queries and reads its whole history. A batched query across the page's milestones would fix that if large repositories find the list slow.

**Sequence diagram:**

1. What user action or system event starts the sequence, and what is the expected outcome when it completes successfully?

   A maintainer opens a repository's Milestones tab, which sends `GET /{owner}/{repo}/milestones`. If it succeeds, every open milestone with enough history shows the chart's projection sentence next to its due date. A late one, for example, reads "Projected to finish on Nov 12, 4 days after the due date" in red. Milestones with too little history show nothing new.

2. Identify the 2--3 most important steps in the sequence. For each one, describe what is happening and note whether it involves existing code or new/modified code from your solution.

   - **Step 8, `burndownOptions(ctx, false)`:** new, but it is existing logic moved out of the chart's handler. It decides once, per request, which kinds of items this viewer's projections may count. Every later step depends on it for AC6.
   - **Steps 9–18, `GetMilestoneBurndown` for each milestone:** existing service, new call site. Calling the same service the chart uses is Decision 1. The service replays the milestone's history from the comment table and computes the 14-day burn rate and projected date, so the list can't disagree with the chart.
   - **Steps 19–23, `NewMilestoneProjection`:** new. It maps the burndown's status to a locale key pair and a day count, or to nil. Steps 26–27 in the modified template then turn that into the sentence with `TrN`, which picks the singular "1 day" form or the plural.

3. What error cases or alternative paths are not shown in the diagram, and why did you leave them out?

   - **The closed tab** (`?state=closed`): the handler skips the whole loop, so no projection is computed (AC4).
   - **A database error inside `GetMilestoneBurndown`:** the handler stops and returns a 500 with `ctx.ServerError`, like the other queries on this page.
   - **A viewer who can read neither issues nor pull requests:** the route rejects them before the handler runs.
   - **A page with no open milestones:** the loop doesn't run.

   I left these out to keep the diagram on the path that the feature changes. Apart from the closed tab, each one is existing behaviour of the page, and the closed tab is just the loop being skipped.

**Cross-cutting:**

4. If you used AI to create or check any part of the diagrams, describe what it produced, what you verified against the actual code, and what you had to correct or add. If AI was not used, write "N/A."

   Claude Code (claude-opus-5-5) drafted both Mermaid sources from the code in PR #134 and rendered them to PNG with the repository's own `mermaid` package in a headless browser. I checked every box, member and call against `routers/web/repo/milestone.go`, `services/issue/milestone_burndown.go`, `services/issue/milestone_projection.go` and `templates/repo/issue/milestones.tmpl`. Corrections made while reviewing the renders:
   - The first sequence draft coloured the whole loop green, which would have marked the existing burndown service as new code. Now only the new projection steps are green, and step 9 says it is a new call to an existing service.
   - A note containing "#14" was cut short, because Mermaid reads `#` as the start of a character code.
   - In the class diagram, a ✎ after `Milestones(ctx)` was shown as a return type.
   - Mermaid's default sizing squeezed the class diagram into an unreadable thumbnail, so it is now rendered at its natural size.

```text
# AI Logs

This folder holds every AI session for each sprint, one folder per student. The course rules are on
the [AI Log Instructions](https://csci-435-se.github.io/ai-logs/) page and the current sprint page
at <https://csci-435-se.github.io/>. This README is the team's shared convention for following them.

## What to log

Every AI session tied to this project: code, debugging, tests, reviews, drafting issues and PRs,
design discussion, the sprint report. That includes sessions that went nowhere. Purely academic
questions unrelated to the project don't need logging.

## Structure

```
ai-logs/
  sprint1/
    <github-username>/                          ← exact GitHub username, matching case
      .gitkeep                                  ← the folder must exist even if you used no AI
      YYYY-MM-DD_<tool>_<short-slug>.md
      YYYY-MM-DD_<tool>_<short-slug>/           ← attachments (images, etc.), optional
```

Team folders: `ab-wm`, `arjunsb26`, `CarsonRackley`, `controlled-opposition`, `Jack-Donohue`,
`vvchopra`.

## Naming

`YYYY-MM-DD_<tool>_<short-slug>.md`

- **Date:** the day the session started.
- **Sprint folder:** the sprint that date falls in, not the sprint the work is for.
- **Tool:** one of the course identifiers: `claude-code`, `claude-web`, `claude-desktop`, `cursor`,
  `gemini-cli`, `codex-cli`, `copilot`, `chatgpt`, `other-<name>`. Claude Code run inside VS Code is
  `claude-code`.
- **Slug:** lowercase words joined with hyphens that say what the session did. Put the issue number
  first when there is one: `issue-52-impl`, `issue-52-spec`, `pr-61-review`, `sprint1-report`.
  Replace auto-generated slugs such as `local-command-caveat...`.
- **Formats:** `.md` is preferred; `.txt` and `.json` are also accepted. No `.docx`, `.pdf`, `.html`
  or share links.

## Capturing a session

| Tool | How |
| --- | --- |
| Claude Code (terminal or VS Code), other agentic CLIs | Start it with [SpecStory](https://specstory.com/): `specstory run claude`, from the repo root. Forgot? Run `specstory sync` afterwards; it back-fills from Claude Code's local history. Then copy from `.specstory/history/` (git-ignored) into your folder and rename it to the convention. |
| Web chat (claude.ai, ChatGPT, Gemini, ...) | Install a browser chat exporter and export the session as Markdown right after it ends. Include any files you pasted in as context. |
| Claude Desktop | SpecStory doesn't capture it. Copy the conversation into a `.md` file by hand. |

At the end of each sprint, run `specstory sync` once more and re-copy. A log copied mid-session is
incomplete.

## Content

- The **tool and AI model** used (SpecStory writes both).
- The **complete** prompt and response history. For agentic tools, that includes file edits and
  commands (SpecStory includes them). Logs with missing responses or truncated histories are
  **invalid**. Don't hand-write, summarise or trim a log; only rename it.
- Attachments (screenshots, snippets) go in a folder with the log's name minus `.md`.
- Log **every** session, including ones that went nowhere. Grading is on how complete the record
  is, not on whether AI helped.

## Where logs are referenced

- **Issue comments only.** Each contributor posts their own `### AI Assistance — @username` comment
  on the issue, with full `https://github.com/...` links to their logs. Format:
  [`.claude-students/AI-ASSISTANCE.md`](../.claude-students/AI-ASSISTANCE.md).
- **Not** in PR descriptions or PR comments. The PR has a short AI-use note with no log link. The
  AI Log Instructions page says "Issue/PR comments", but the Sprint 1 page narrows this to issue
  comments only, and the sprint page wins.
- Each teammate posts their own comment, including reviewers who used AI to review.
- No AI used? Post an issue comment saying so, and keep your folder with its `.gitkeep`.
- The sprint report lists each member's tools, session count, folder link, and 2–3 sentences on
  lessons learned.
